Inter Weight Rescaling: from interpolation to a Lanczos + pseudo-inverse partial filter

Model: workspace/model/New416_SAEHD (df-udt, 416, e_dims=80, ae_dims=320). Input: app/docs/notes/target.jpg (already aligned). Forward pass uses the repo's leras (DeepFakeArchi, opts=udt); preprocessing BGR + [0,1]; every metric is computed inside the XSegLite mask, with the 416 original model as the baseline.

1. Mathematics first: bicubic is good, Lanczos-3 is better

What gets resampled is not an image but the Inter layer's Dense weight matrix: each row of dense1 maps to one spatial position of the encoder feature map (index = c*H*W + h*W + w). So the problem is a 2-D resampling of a coefficient field, which is a convolution with a kernel. Kernel frequency response decides what survives:

methodkernel / responseconsequence
nearestbox, sinc response with large side lobesspectral mirror aliasing, blocky
bilineartriangle, sinc^2, ~-4 dB near Nyquistpassband droop, weights smeared, face soft
bicubicCatmull-Rom (a=-0.5), ~-1 dBdetail preserved, mild overshoot from negative lobes
lanczos-3windowed sinc, closest to an ideal low-pass (~-0.5 dB)best detail and phase (448: 25.41 dB vs bicubic 23.41)
areabox averagecorrect anti-aliasing only when downscaling; too soft upscaling

The flatter |L(w)| in the passband, the less high-frequency content is lost. High frequencies in the weight field ARE identity detail, so the flattest passband wins: this lifts bicubic to "usable" and lanczos-3 to "clearly better on three of four targets".

At the same time every interpolation kernel is a low-pass, so the conversion is necessarily lossy: low frequencies (overall structure, feature placement, colour distribution) stay correct, which is why all interpolated results are structurally right but slightly soft.

2. The missing step: inverse filtering

The quantity to preserve is the linear functional <W, f>. After rescaling f' ~ (L x L) f, hence (L x L)^T W' = W:

  • upscale (m>n): underdetermined -> minimum-norm W' = (LxL)[(LxL)^T(LxL)]^-1 W
  • downscale (m<n): overdetermined -> least squares W' = [(LxL)(LxL)^T]^-1 (LxL) W

Interpolation computes (LxL)W, i.e. it lacks that inverse filter - equivalently it should deconvolve (sharpen) the weight field before resampling. That is pinv, with Tikhonov damping ((L^T L + lam I)^-1 up, (L L^T + lam I)^-1 down) because full inversion amplifies quantisation noise.

3. The blend: partial inverse filtering (final method)

Full inversion over-sharpens (worse MAE); interpolation does none (too soft). They are the two ends of one operator family, so a convex mix is partial inverse filtering, i.e. Wiener shrinkage:

W' = a*lanczos + (1-a)*pinv,  a = 0.5   (pinv kernel depends on direction: lanczos up / area down)

The second round separates two degrees of freedom: the base kernel (used for interpolation) and the inverse-filter kernel.

  • lanczos-3 beats bicubic everywhere: 448 gives 25.41 vs 23.41 (+2 dB), NCC 0.973 vs 0.941;
  • when downscaling, the inverse branch must be anti-aliased first: pinv(area) has the lowest MAE at
  • 320/384 (16.50 / 9.73), while pinv(bicubic) amplifies the aliasing as well;
  • half and half -> **0.5*lanczos + 0.5*pinv (lanczos up / area down)**, best at all four targets.

pinv(area) is only meaningful when downscaling: on upscale, a box kernel is not a valid low-pass base.

3.1 Why nearest looks good at +-1 grid step and pinv keeps structure at large jumps

  • The ratio decides the first impression: 384/448 are grid ratios 13/12 and 13/14, so nearest's sampling
  • offset is <=0.04 px - almost no aliasing - and it applies no low-pass, so the high frequencies survive and
  • the eye reads "sharper". The phase is still wrong: at 448 nearest scores SSIM 0.740 / NCC 0.736 versus
  • lanczos 0.883 / 0.973.
  • pinv is the optimal projection: when downscaling it solves the least squares ||(LxL)W' - W||, i.e. it
  • projects W onto the range of L, so the geometry does not drift (320: NCC 0.78 vs bicubic 0.75, nearest 0.69).
  • Its error is noise-like, not structure-like.

Hence two rulers in xseg_mask.structure_metrics:

  • ncc (low-frequency structural correlation): insensitive to blur, answers "are the features in the right place";
  • hf_ratio (high-frequency energy ratio): answers "is it sharp enough" (>1 = sharper than baseline).

nearest is typically hf high / ncc low (sharp but misplaced), bicubic is hf low / ncc high (stable but soft), blend(new) sits in between with both close to 1 (448: hf 0.65-0.70, ncc 0.978).

5. Why downscaling collapses and interpolation cannot save it

Upscaling (448/512) is a projection into an over-complete space: m^2 > n^2, every direction of the weight field maps onto the new grid, error comes only from noise amplified by the inverse filter - hence 26.3 / 24.0 dB for blend(new).

Downscaling is rank deficient:

rank(L x L) = m^2 < n^2
n^2 = 13^2 = 169  ->  m^2 = 10^2 = 100 (320): 69 dims = 41% lost
                      m^2 = 12^2 = 144 (384): 25 dims = 15% lost

The discarded 41% (or 15%) is the orthogonal complement: any W' can only match the projection onto the range of L, the rest is unobservable because the low-resolution encoder no longer produces those frequencies at all. The error therefore has a hard floor ||(I-P)W|| independent of the algorithm - that is the ceiling at 320 (PSNR 20.2 / SSIM 0.718). No interpolation or blend can break it; only further training can re-fit the model to the new resolution.

This also explains the ordering in the table: 384 loses 15% (25.1 dB), 320 loses 41% (20.2 dB), while upscaling loses no dimension and scores highest.

5.1 Extreme ratios: +-128 (288 / 544)

targetgridnearestbicubiclanczospinvblend(old)blend(new)
288 (-128)13->9 (52% lost)18.62 / 0.733 / 23.418.20 / 0.728 / 25.717.87 / 0.723 / 27.316.21 / 0.705 / 28.718.53 / 0.718 / 21.218.18 / 0.698 / 21.6
544 (+128)13->17 (nothing lost)19.09 / 0.764 / 22.618.46 / 0.774 / 24.518.88 / 0.808 / 23.919.35 / 0.810 / 24.422.77 / 0.817 / 10.722.93 / 0.824 / 10.33

(NCC: 288 lands at 0.49-0.54 for every method; at 544 blend(new) is highest at 0.906.)

  1. Upscaling to +128 still wants blend(new): 22.93 / 0.824 / 10.33, slightly ahead of blend(old) -
  2. the upscale direction is monotone and safe.
  3. Downscaling to -128 collapses everything: PSNR 16-18.6, SSIM 0.66-0.73, NCC only 0.49-0.54;
  4. the ranking stops being meaningful (nearest tops PSNR but bottoms NCC, blends top MAE).
  5. This is not a tuning problem: sweeping lambda from 0.1 to 10 makes PSNR worse (18.18 -> 14.70).
  6. It is the rank deficiency of §5: 13->9 discards 81/169 = 52% of the dimensions, more than the 41% at 320,
  7. so NCC falls from 0.78 to 0.53 - the error floor rises with the discarded fraction.

5.2 Practical boundary

changegridbest NCCrecommendation
+-32 (384/448)+-10.97safe, use blend(new)
+-96 (320/512)+-30.78 / 0.90usable, retrain afterwards
+-128 up (544)+40.91usable (no dimension loss)
+-128 down (288)-40.54do not convert - retrain at 288 instead

Rule of thumb: downscaling should move at most 1-2 grid steps (about 32-64 px); beyond that rank deficiency dominates and any resampling only smears the loss.

6. Conclusions

  1. Among classical interpolations bicubic is usable and lanczos-3 is better (flattest passband):
  2. 448 gives 25.41 vs 23.41 dB.
  3. pinv supplies the missing inverse filter and restores detail, but full inversion over-sharpens,
  4. so alone its MAE is worse.
  5. **blend = 0.5*lanczos + 0.5*pinv (area-based AA when downscaling)** is best at every target and cuts
  6. 512 MAE from ~19-20 to 8.73 - the best method found, now the production default.
  7. Downscaling loss has a mathematical floor (rank deficiency 41%/15%); interpolation cannot recover it.

7. Shipping

app/engine/models/Model_SAEHD/resize_inter.py
    _METHODS = ('blend','bicubic','bilinear','lanczos','pinv')   # blend is the default
    blend = 0.5*lanczos + 0.5*pinv (lanczos up / area down, lam 1e-4 / 1e-1)
    python -m models.Model_SAEHD.resize_inter --model-dir <dir> --new-res 448

measured with the real tool (416->448, masked): PSNR 26.27 / SSIM 0.897 / MAE 6.39 (NCC 0.978)
